title: Study Abroad Report: Medical University of Vienna
paragraphs: Through the Nagoya University exchange program, I studied abroad at the Medical University of Vienna for about three months. I applied to the program simply because I was interested in medicine outside Japan, not with the purpose of building a foothold for working overseas in the future. Even so, I sensed even before departure that this study abroad would surely be an experience beyond compare. In my study abroad I rotated through the ER for the first three weeks, GP for the next four weeks, and thoracic surgery for the last four weeks. My biggest worry was of course the problem of language, so I remember being full of tension as I faced my first day of clerkship in the ER. That worry came true exactly, and on the first day the boss of the ER dismissed me, saying, "If you can't speak German, I'm sorry, but it will be observation only. If you can't speak English more smoothly and fluently, you're no use." In the end my ER clerkship was almost entirely observation, and I was not entrusted with examining patients or performing procedures. Even so, when I did not understand something I looked it up on the spot myself or asked the ER doctors, so even just watching was educational.

The next, GP, is in English general practitioner, a department where one learns medicine for family doctors. Europe, North America and some Asian countries have adopted the family doctor system, so doctors who wish to become family doctors in the future study in this department for several years. It plays a role close to that of the general medicine department in Japan. In the kind of doctor I aim to be in the future, there is a doctor who can see any disease evenly and a doctor who can provide whole-person medicine. For that reason I was strongly interested in the family doctor, who plays the role of a so-called jack of all trades, and I chose this department. Here, on weekdays you do a clerkship at a family doctor's office in the city of Vienna (something like the primary care clerkship in the polyclinic), and you can also visit various medical facilities in Austria. In my case, I was able to visit many medical facilities, such as a homeless care center, an HIV health care center, a night emergency visiting service center, an STD prevention center and a long-term care health facility. I was told that if there were other facilities I wanted to visit, they would readily add them to the schedule.

And on weekends you stay overnight and do a clerkship with a family doctor in the Austrian countryside. What stayed in my memory about GP was of course the weekend clerkship. Here you can immerse yourself fully in rural European medicine and life. I saw various cases, from diseases peculiar to the countryside, such as orthopedic diseases from too much farm work and farmer's lung, to pregnancy and pediatrics. On holidays, in the event of an accident such as a traffic accident, the family doctor was the first to be dispatched, performing lifesaving care even before the ambulance, and I was able to help with that. In addition, I was served home cooking of the region for meals and was allowed to experience things that one cannot ordinarily experience. In this way, the clerkship in the countryside was very meaningful, and I truly felt from the bottom of my heart that I was glad I had studied abroad. Perhaps because the GP clerkship was originally a program for exchange students, it was educational for exchange students, and they answered our questions kindly and tried to draw questions out of us.

Finally, thoracic surgery. I was also interested in surgery myself, and after hesitating between thoracic surgery, which has more transplants than in Japan, and cardiac surgery, I chose thoracic surgery. The daily schedule was a morning conference at 7 lasting about an hour, and after that I could move around freely as I wished, drawing blood and placing IV lines in ward work, joining operation observation, and observing outpatient clinics. Since I was interested in surgery, I actively observed operations every day and was able to observe a lung transplant, which was my original goal, and because it was also chest surgery, I was fortunate to be able to observe a heart transplant, which is performed only a few times a year even in Japan.

I was able to have such valuable experiences thanks to Dr. 粕谷 and Ms. 山崎 of the International Exchange Office, the staff of the academic affairs office, the doctors of the Frontier Society, the doctors who looked after me during my clerkship in Vienna, the seniors who supported me in various ways before my study abroad, and my classmates. I take this opportunity to express my deep gratitude. Thank you very much.
